title: Quantum Computers will constrain the Equation of State of Neutron Stars
authors: Adrián Castaño-García, Nahia J. Dios-Bilbao, J. J. Gálvez-Viruet, Felipe J. Llanes-Estrada, Marío Logrosán-Álvarez, Nicolás M. Arenaza, María Gómez-Rocha
abstract: The Equation of State (EoS) of Nuclear Matter at high densities, and particularly that of neutron stars, resists $\mathit{ab}$ $\mathit{initio}$ Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) computations due to the notorious sign problem of Lattice Gauge Theory at finite chemical potential. A quantum computer deploying QCD in canonical quantization should be able to make substantial progress. We set some basic goals for a future quantum computer to predict the EoS, and thus the basic static observables of the star (mass, radius and Tidal deformability, for example). We then develop the basic theory to address the canonical Hamiltonian in Weyl (time-axial) gauge expressed in normal modes, together with the squared Gauss operator $\mathcal{G}^2$ necessary to execute energy minimization algorithms restricted to the physical Fock subspace. Finally, we deploy our particle-quantum register encoding of a generic field theory to demonstrate QCD at finite chemical potential for a few (three-four) particles with a modest number of momentum modes, by simulating the quantum computer on a classical cluster. This opens the possibility for effective quantum computers to constrain the microscopic physics of neutron stars simultaneously to the operation of third--generation gravitational wave detectors such as the Einstein Telescope, providing more detailed predictions than has been possible until now.
summary: This paper outlines a quantum computing approach to solve the intractable problem of determining the Equation of State (EoS) for matter inside neutron stars. By developing a theoretical framework based on QCD Hamiltonian simulation, they show how future quantum computers could drastically reduce uncertainties in key astrophysical observables like stellar radius and tidal deformability. This bridges high-energy nuclear theory with advanced quantum computation techniques.
main_problem: The primary challenge is determining the Equation of State (EoS) for ultra-dense nuclear matter, specifically within neutron stars, which is intractable using standard Lattice QCD due to the sign problem.
main_result: The authors propose that future quantum computers can constrain the EoS by simulating QCD at finite chemical potential, leading to significantly reduced uncertainties in key observables like radius and tidal deformability.
method: They develop a theoretical framework for solving the canonical Hamiltonian of QCD in Weyl gauge on a quantum computer architecture, using variational minimization techniques.
model_or_system: The system is Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) applied to neutron star cores. The theory focuses on developing the Hamiltonian formalism and encoding quark-gluon states onto qubit registers for simulation.
key_observables: Static observables of neutron stars: mass, radius ($R$), and Tidal deformability ($\Lambda$). Derived quantities include energy density ($ho$) and pressure ($p$).
important_parameters: High densities (intermediate regimes) where classical QCD fails; the coupling constant $g$; specific quark/gluon configurations (e.g., 3 quarks, 1 gluon).
main_assumptions: The work is a proof-of-concept demonstration limited to small particle numbers (e.g., three quarks and one gluon) due to current computational constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the narrowing of uncertainty bands for EoS observables when constrained by quantum computation, comparing theoretical predictions with existing bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical problem (EoS difficulty) to developing the necessary Hamiltonian theory in canonical gauge, detailing the quantum encoding and minimization procedure, and finally demonstrating the method via simulation results.
why_interesting: While focused on nuclear astrophysics, the core methodology involves mapping a complex field theory Hamiltonian onto a qubit register for variational energy minimization, which is highly relevant to simulating strongly correlated many-body systems in general.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Top panel: Uncertainty band for the EoS P(ρ). EoS min/max are the lower/upper bounds (below an even- tual first order phase transition) while respecting stability (cs ≥0)/causality (cs ≤1) once microscopic physics has been accounted , at both low and high ρ. Bottom: Eventual improvement of the EoS to narrow the current band, which quantum computer investigations should aim to achieve.

FIG. 2. Top panel: Mass (in solar masses) against neutron- star radius. Bottom: Mass against Tidal deformability. The extreme lines show the current prediction of these observables excluding astrophysical constraints, from microscopic theory alone. The intermediate lines, from the left bottom corner towards the right and up, represent the improved predictions if one (ρ, P) point is calculated at the densities marked in the bottom plot of Fig. 1 (note that their uncertainty bands are anchored at the stiffest EoS, so they lift the softest one).

FIG. 3. Energies obtained after applying Eq. (67) to the mini- mum of the expectation value of the Hamiltonian constrained by Gauss’ law. We see no sensitivity to changing the fitting procedure, “Exp” denoting an exponential function fit, see Eq. (72) and “Fraction” a fit with a fraction of polynomi- als, see Eq. (73). We do see strong sensitivity to the trial variational wavefunction. This is expected, and a working large-scale quantum computer, with its massive Hilbert space, would be the tool to address it.

FIG. 4. Pressure and sound velocity squared as functions of the energy density, obtained from the minimum of the time- axial QCD Hamiltonian expectation value evaluated with the variational wavefunction described in Sec. IV A 1 and IV A 2, and after applying Eq. (67).
